metadata.audience: makers following the channel's Claude + Walker game workflows

beats.narration_text: Hola, this is Liam, in for Bear. This is how Walker is meant to be asked: hand it a game design document, get back a playable Godot project. The prompt on screen is a reconstruction, not a transcript, because this game was built first, and its document came after.

props.command: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about Basketball Blaster: Fowl Play — Mr. Block, armed with a basketball gun and basketball grenades, collects every egg across three arenas while chickens pour out of pipes — into a playable Godot project.
props.runningText: illustrative reconstruction — not the historical prompt
output: What happened: a Unity arena shooter was ported to Godot first.
GDD.md was written afterwards, from the folder's own evidence.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: The Design Document

beats.narration_text: Basketball Blaster came before its design document. It ports a Unity arena shooter to Godot and stretches it to three arenas. The document was written last, from the evidence, and nothing in it is signed off.

props.text:
Basketball Blaster
was built from its GDD.
Nothing is signed off.

show.event: BrutalistHesitantWriter:

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant writer: text is typed on screen over the narration, so mid-beat samples legitimately show a partial page. The finished six-line text fills the safe area and holds for the last 1.5 s.

beats.narration_text: Before anything else, the document refuses to let one word mean two things. Every claim wears a label: recovered from the Unity code, stated in the README, invented for the port, built, seen in a capture, or still waiting on a human. The build runs end to end: eight scenes, two scripted takes, fifty-nine assertions passing. Zero human playtests. Both are true at once.

portrait_card.reason: native 9:16 large-type card; shared 916 board fine print is below the GATE T portrait floor
portrait_card.title: How the Document Labels a Claim

show.event: portrait card: How the Document Labels a Claim

beats.narration_text: Section two admits a gap. The README says what was ported and what was added, but no document says who this game is for, or why anyone should play it. So the vision line on screen is the agent's proposal, and it's marked that way. The three pillars are read off the code: eggs end a level, kills never do; the arena is vertical; and every hit is loud.

portrait_card.reason: native 9:16 large-type card; shared 916 board fine print is below the GATE T portrait floor
portrait_card.title: A Vision Nobody Wrote Down

show.event: portrait card: A Vision Nobody Wrote Down

beats.narration_text: Here's the core loop, on the real build, played by a script. He's just lost a life to the flock, and respawns at the gate. Then he heads for the nearest nest, shooting whatever is close, and each egg ticks the counter. The fifth egg ends the arena: court cleared. Notice what decided it. Eggs. Kills never end a level.

beats.narration_text: Experience goals are where a design document starts guessing, so all four are labelled proposed. And the captures already push back on two of them. The autopilot collected every egg in under twenty seconds per arena. Fighting in place for twenty-five seconds earned ten kills, cost a life, and collected nothing. On this build, rushing beats fighting. That's not a playtest. It's a reason to run one.

portrait_card.reason: native 9:16 large-type card; shared 916 board fine print is below the GATE T portrait floor
portrait_card.title: Goals Nobody Has Approved

show.event: portrait card: Goals Nobody Has Approved

beats.narration_text: Mechanics, and one honest discovery. The Unity project declared a jetpack input, a single true-or-false field, and no script ever read it. The port wires it up: hold Shift, burn one point six seconds of fuel, rise at up to four hundred and thirty pixels a second. That's new, so the document labels it authored, not recovered. Two quieter retunes get the same label: coyote time and the fire rate.

portrait_card.reason: native 9:16 large-type card; shared 916 board fine print is below the GATE T portrait floor
portrait_card.title: The Jetpack Unity Never Wired Up

show.event: portrait card: The Jetpack Unity Never Wired Up

beats.narration_text: In play. A walk, a jump, then a second press in mid-air: the double jump launches him again. Shift lights the jetpack, and the blue fuel bar drains. The gun follows the crosshair and fires a ball every four tenths of a second. Right-click lobs a grenade: three beeps, then the blast. And watch the health balls, top left. Chickens tag him twice during the demo.

beats.narration_text: The mega kill comes straight from the Unity audio manager: three or more chickens dying before the next physics frame. The port keeps the number and the rule. In practice it means a grenade, landed in a crowd. The capture got one.

portrait_card.reason: native 9:16 large-type card; shared 916 board fine print is below the GATE T portrait floor

show.event: portrait card: Three at Once

beats.narration_text: Fight phase. He comes in with one health ball and loses a life almost at once. Then a grenade lands among four chickens: mega kill. Here it is again at a quarter of the speed, labelled as a replay, not a second run. The idea is simple: hold one spot, shoot, and lob grenades at clusters.

beats.narration_text: Damage is forgiving by design. A touch costs one of three health and buys a second of invulnerability. Three hits cost a life, and you respawn at the gate with two seconds of safety. Before you reappear, any chicken camping the gate is deleted. That last rule isn't in the Unity code. It's the port's own fairness patch.

portrait_card.title: How Forgiving a Hit Is

show.event: portrait card: How Forgiving a Hit Is

beats.narration_text: Now the failure path, on purpose. The driver walks into the flock without firing. Three hits, a fade to navy, and a respawn at the gate. Again. And again. With the third life gone, the defeat screen asks: the flock won arena one, run it back? Retry Arena loads the same court with all three lives restored.

beats.narration_text: Under the hood, two choices matter. Contact damage isn't a physics collision. Every frame, the arena measures the distance from Mister Block to each chicken. And there are no automated tests at all. The only machine checks are this film's: a smoke run of all eight scenes, and the assertions inside the two scripted takes.

portrait_card.reason: native 9:16 large-type card; shared 916 board fine print is below the GATE T portrait floor
portrait_card.title: No Tests, One Distance Check

show.event: portrait card: No Tests, One Distance Check

beats.narration_text: Progression is one table. Each arena is wider, with more pipes, faster spawns, a higher cap and more eggs, and arena three's chickens take four hits. Whether that feels harder is a human question. The captures can only say the autopilot needed about thirteen, fourteen, then nineteen seconds.

portrait_card.title: Difficulty Is One Table

beats.narration_text: Arena two, Sunset Rooftops: three pipes, an orange tint, six eggs. Cut to arena three, the Fowl Play Finals: four pipes, a darker navy tint, seven eggs, and one more platform row near the ceiling.

beats.narration_text: The story is eight lines long: a pre-game briefing where the coach explains the controls and Mister Block says, let's ball. Unity had none of it. The rest of the interface is a main menu, how to play, a pause screen, and the end cards. And the briefing is where the first defect lives.

portrait_card.reason: native 9:16 large-type card; shared 916 board fine print is below the GATE T portrait floor
portrait_card.title: Eight Lines of Story

show.event: portrait card: Eight Lines of Story

beats.narration_text: The prompt says enter or click to continue. Watch the click on the dialogue box: nothing. Above it: nothing. Enter works, and Escape skips. The reason: a full-screen shade layer swallows every click before the briefing can see it. It's small, but it's the first thing a new player touches.

beats.narration_text: Every sound and the music loop were synthesized for the port, because the Unity export had no audio files. The art is the Unity project's, cropped and sliced. Who owns it, and whether it can be published, isn't written down anywhere. Out of scope, by omission: saves, settings, accessibility options, online play.

portrait_card.reason: native 9:16 large-type card; shared 916 board fine print is below the GATE T portrait floor
portrait_card.title: Whose Art Is This?

show.event: portrait card: Whose Art Is This?

beats.narration_text: Section fifteen lists what the captures found: the dead click, and HUD hints drawn over their own bars. Then six open questions only a person can answer. Who is this for? Should fighting pay? Are the retunes intended? Who owns the art? The appendices hold the acceptance table, with one row still empty: a human playtest.

portrait_card.reason: native 9:16 large-type card; shared 916 board fine print is below the GATE T portrait floor
portrait_card.title: What a Person Still Has to Decide

show.event: portrait card: What a Person Still Has to Decide

beats.narration_text: Verdict. This document organizes; it doesn't approve. What's built is observed working end to end, with fifty-nine machine assertions behind it. What it found is concrete: a dead click, overlapping hints, and a loop where eggs beat fighting. What's left belongs to a person: the purpose, the art rights, the feel, and whether it's worth playing at all.

portrait_card.reason: native 9:16 large-type card; shared 916 board fine print is below the GATE T portrait floor
portrait_card.title: Verdict

show.event: portrait card: Verdict

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude with your own design document: Here is my game's design document. Pick one proposed experience goal. Rewrite it as a hypothesis with a test I can run with three players, and tell me which result would make me change the design. If no result would change your mind, it isn't a hypothesis yet. Liam, in for Bear.
